Dynamic: yes — long-run supernormal profit gives both the means and the motive to invest in R&D, the monopolist's strongest defence.

old:
A contestable market is one with freedom of entry and exit. What disciplines firms is the threat of potential competition, not the number of firms currently in the market.

The distinction: competition is about how many firms there are; contestability is about how easily firms can enter and leave. A concentrated market can still behave competitively if it is highly contestable — Amazon and eBay both do.

old:
Rather than profit-maximising at MC = MR, the incumbent sets price down at the output where AR = AC, earning only normal profit — the same point a sales-maximiser chooses.

With no supernormal profit on display, there is no profit signal to attract entrants. The more contestable the market, the closer behaviour drifts towards the perfectly competitive outcome: lower prices, higher output, greater allocative efficiency.

old:
Sunk costs are costs that cannot be recovered if a firm leaves the market — specialised machinery, advertising, research and development.

They are the main barrier to exit: the higher they are, the riskier entry becomes, so the less contestable the market. Other barriers work on the way in — economies of scale, high start-up costs, legal barriers, brand loyalty, control of key resources and anti-competitive practices.

old:
MRP = MPP × MR. Marginal physical product (MPP) is the extra output produced by one more worker; marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue gained from selling that extra output.

The MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour, D(L) — and it slopes downward because of the law of diminishing returns.

old:
Labour demand responds more to wage changes when: the final product's demand is price elastic, so wage-driven price rises lose many sales; capital can easily substitute for labour; and labour is a large share of total costs, so a wage change moves total costs significantly.

It is also more elastic over a longer time period, when firms have time to reorganise production.

old:
Geographical immobility — workers cannot move to where the jobs are (house prices and rent, transport costs, information gaps). Occupational immobility — skills do not transfer between industries (training and qualification requirements, technological change).

Both leave vacancies unfilled beside workers unemployed: structural unemployment and skill shortages. Policy answers: education, apprenticeships and careers guidance for occupational mobility; subsidised housing, relocation help and better transport for geographical.

old:
It depends on the size of the rise: far above equilibrium means big income gains but substantial real wage unemployment. It depends on the wage elasticity of labour demand: with inelastic demand few jobs are lost, so the policy works best where demand is wage inelastic.

And it depends on motivation: if higher pay lifts productivity, the rise in firms' average costs — and the job losses — shrink. The elasticities of labour demand and supply decide how any labour market intervention plays out.

old:
For: shareholder pressure creates a profit incentive that can drive productive efficiency, lower prices, and — through reinvested profit — dynamic efficiency and better quality. Against: the firm no longer exists to serve everyone; with weak competition it may raise prices and cut quality.

The verdict turns on competition and contestability (parcel delivery, yes; water, no) and on the effectiveness of regulation — which itself depends on avoiding regulatory capture.

old:
Suppliers facing a monopsony buyer: minimum prices (a legal price floor), support for cooperatives so suppliers can bargain together, and merger control to stop monopsony power growing.

Employees: the national minimum wage, employment legislation (health and safety, working hours, unfair dismissal), support for trade unions, and pay transparency requirements that pressure employers towards fair wages.

  • Support for cooperatives so suppliers can bargain together.
  • Merger control to stop monopsony power growing.

Employees:

  • The national minimum wage.
  • Employment legislation (health and safety, working hours, unfair dismissal).
  • Support for trade unions.
  • Pay transparency requirements that pressure employers towards fair wages.

old:
Prices: lower, so essentials stay affordable at every income. Quality: higher, through investment and innovation. Choice: wider, improving allocative efficiency. Profit: controlled — enough to fund reinvestment, not extracted at consumers' expense. Efficiency: better productive and allocative efficiency.

Every intervention in 3.6.1 is judged against these five yardsticks.

old:
Regulatory capture: regulated firms gain so much influence over their regulator that the rules end up shaped in the firms' favour rather than consumers'.

Two causes: asymmetric information — the regulator depends on the firm's own data, which the firm can present selectively — and the "revolving door", where regulators soften rules hoping for future jobs in the industry. The result is regulation that is too lenient to bite.

old:
Asymmetric information: regulators know less than the firms they police, so policies end up poorly targeted, easy to dodge or costly. Administrative costs can exceed the benefits. Unintended consequences: caps and rules can choke innovation, quality or competition. Conflicting objectives: a price cap that helps consumers today can starve investment tomorrow.

When intervention makes the outcome worse than the market failure it targeted, that is government failure.
